question: Which one of the following statements is not correct?
opt_a: Real GDP is calculated by valuing outputs of different years at common prices.
opt_b: Potential GDP is the real GDP that the economy would produce if its resources were fully employed.
opt_c: Nominal GDP is calculated by valuing outputs of different years at constant prices.
opt_d: Real GDP per capita is the ratio of real GDP divided by population.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Nominal GDP is calculated by valuing outputs of different years at constant prices. That sentence describes real GDP , not nominal GDP, and this swap is what the item is built around. The school text is explicit on both halves: 'Real GDP is calculated in a way such that the goods and services are evaluated at some constant set of prices (or constant prices)', while 'Nominal GDP, on the other hand, is simply the value of GDP at the current prevailing prices.' The distinction is the point of national-income accounting. Hold prices fixed at a base year and any movement in the total must come from the volume of output, so real GDP measures production. Let prices run at each year's own level and the total moves with prices as well as output, which is why nominal GDP can rise in a year when nothing extra was produced.

question: The mismatch in the regional or occupational pattern of job vacancies and the pattern of worker availability results in
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Structural unemployment. The stem is a definition, and the two words that carry it are 'mismatch' and 'pattern'. Structural unemployment is involuntary unemployment caused by a mismatch between the skills workers can offer and the skills employers are demanding, and, in the regional version the stem also names, between where the vacancies are and where the workers are. The jobs exist and the workers exist; they simply do not fit each other. That is why this kind of unemployment is stubborn. It cannot be cured by boosting demand, because more spending does not turn a retrenched jute-mill hand in Howrah into a data-centre technician in Hyderabad. What it takes is retraining, or migration, or both, and both take years, which is why structural spells last far longer than the short gap between one job and the next.

question: The situation in an economy which is growing slowly along with rapid inflation (rising price level) is called
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Stagflation. The word is a portmanteau of stagnation and inflation , and it names exactly the pairing in the stem: output crawling while prices race. The pairing was long thought impossible. The orthodox reading of the Phillips curve held that inflation and unemployment traded off against each other, so slack growth was supposed to come with easing prices. The rich economies of the 1970s got both at once after the oil shocks, and the word entered the textbooks to describe it. The mechanism usually invoked is a supply shock: when the cost of an input that everything depends on jumps, firms produce less and charge more at the same time. That is also why stagflation is hard to treat: tightening money to bring prices down deepens the slowdown, and loosening it to support growth feeds the inflation.

question: The increase in private investment spending induced by the increase in Government spending is known as
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Crowding in. The stem gives the direction plainly: government spending goes up and private investment goes up with it, induced by the public spending rather than squeezed by it. That is the crowding-in case. Two channels are usually named for it. The first is demand: in an economy with idle capacity, public spending raises incomes, sales pick up, and firms that had shelved projects find them worth doing after all. The second is infrastructure: a road, a port or a power line built with public money lowers the cost of private production along that corridor and makes investments profitable that were not profitable before. Both leave private capital formation higher than it would have been, which is precisely what the sentence describes. Note the two-word trap built into the option list: crowding in and crowding out sit next to each other and differ by one word, and they name opposite effects.

question: The asset or assets that a borrower pledges in order to guarantee repayment of a loan is called as
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Collateral. The stem is a near-quotation of the school definition: collateral is an asset that the borrower owns (land, a building, a vehicle, livestock, a deposit with a bank) and uses as a guarantee to the lender until the loan is repaid. If the borrower fails to repay, the lender may sell that asset to recover the money. Security of this kind is what makes lending possible to a stranger, and it is also why the poorest borrowers are the hardest to lend to: not owning a titled asset, they cannot offer the guarantee that formal lenders ask for, which pushes them towards informal moneylenders on much worse terms. Collateral is one item in a larger package. Interest rate, collateral, documentation requirement and the mode of repayment together make up what is called the terms of credit, and those terms vary sharply between a bank and a village lender.

question: The percentage by which the money the borrower pays back exceeds the money that was borrowed is called as
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Nominal interest rate. The stem measures the excess of repayment over principal in money terms, rupees back against rupees lent, and that is exactly what the nominal rate is: the rate written into the loan agreement and the one the borrower actually hands over. 'Nominal' means counted in money, without any correction for what has happened to prices. Borrow Rs 100 and repay Rs 110 and the nominal rate is ten per cent, whatever inflation was that year. The real rate is what is left after that correction, and it is not what the stem describes.

question: Which one of the following statements about the Gandhi-Irwin Pact of 1931 is correct?
opt_a: The Government would not release those prisoners who had been non-violent.
opt_b: The Government would not release those prisoners who had indulged in the peaceful picketing of liquor and foreign cloth shops.
opt_c: The Congress did not agree to the suspension of the Civil Disobedience Movement.
opt_d: The Congress agreed to take part in the Second Round Table Conference.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, The Congress agreed to take part in the Second Round Table Conference. That was the heart of the bargain struck in Delhi on 5 March 1931. The Congress had boycotted the first Round Table Conference; the pact brought it in for the second, with Gandhi going to London later that year as the sole Congress representative. The other three options invert what the pact actually contained. On the Government's side it undertook to release political prisoners other than those guilty of violence, to withdraw the ordinances and prosecutions brought against the Civil Disobedience Movement, to return confiscated property of satyagrahis, to allow people on the coast to make salt for their own use, and to permit peaceful picketing of liquor and foreign cloth shops. On the Congress side it undertook to discontinue civil disobedience and to attend the conference. Read the four options against that list and only the last survives.

question: Who among the following founded the Bhil Seva Mandal in 1922?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Amritlal Vithaldas Thakkar. Known everywhere as Thakkar Bapa, he founded the Bhil Seva Mandal in 1922. He had come to social work by an unusual route: trained as a civil engineer, he worked on railway and municipal projects before joining Gokhale's Servants of India Society in 1914 and giving the rest of his life to relief and tribal welfare. The Bhil Seva Mandal took him into the Bhil country of the Panchmahals and the Dangs, where he ran schools, hostels and famine relief among a community the colonial administration had classified and policed rather than served. His work made him the person the national movement turned to on tribal questions: he later became general secretary of the Harijan Sevak Sangh, which Gandhi set up in 1932, and he is credited with putting the word Adivasi into general use for India's tribal peoples.

question: In 1911, who among the following introduced a bill in the Imperial Legislative Council for introduction of compulsory and free primary education in India?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Gopal Krishna Gokhale. As a member of the Imperial Legislative Council he carried the cause of compulsory free primary education into legislation. William Wedderburn, in an account published in 1913, refers plainly to reformers 'supporting Mr. Gokhale's Bill in the Viceroy's Council for free and compulsory elementary education.' The proposal fitted everything else he did. Elected president of the Congress in 1905, he founded the Servants of India Society in that same year with the expansion of Indian education as its central purpose; the Society went on to run mobile libraries, found schools and hold night classes for factory workers. The bill was nevertheless defeated. The official reasoning offered against it, which UPSC has itself set as an examinable point, was that literacy among cultivators would breed discontent.

question: Which one of the following statements about the Act V of 1843 relating to Slavery in India is correct?
opt_a: It gave the masters the right to wilfully keep their slaves tied to their estates.
opt_b: It denied the masters the use of Courts to assert their claims on slaves.
opt_c: The Law Courts and masters worked jointly in resolving the cases of desertion.
opt_d: The slaves became the owners of the land.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, It denied the masters the use of Courts to assert their claims on slaves. That is what the statute actually does, almost in those words. Section 2 of Act V of 1843 provides that no rights arising out of an alleged property in the person and services of another as a slave shall be enforced by any civil or criminal court or magistrate within the territories of the East India Company. The Act came into force on 7 April 1843. The reform did not declare slaves free, seize anyone's holdings or make slave-owning a crime. It withdrew the state's machinery : a master who wanted a runaway returned could no longer have the claim enforced in court, because the law would not recognise the property he was asserting. Slavery was left without legal standing, which in practice hollowed it out; making it a punishable offence in its own right waited for the Indian Penal Code of 1860.

question: Which Maratha statesman signed the Treaty of Bassein on December 31, 1802?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Baji Rao II. The treaty was a pact between the British East India Company and Baji Rao II, the Peshwa, signed at Bassein (modern Vasai, north of Bombay) on the last day of 1802. He had reached the coast as a fugitive: Yashwantrao Holkar had beaten the combined forces of the Peshwa and Sindhia outside Poona that October, and Baji Rao fled to British protection and bought it at the price the Company named. The terms were the standard subsidiary alliance in its heaviest form. A permanent force of about six thousand Company troops was to be stationed with him; districts yielding some twenty-six lakh rupees were made over to pay for them; he renounced claims on Surat and Baroda; Europeans other than the British were barred from his service; and he agreed to make no treaty, declare no war and conduct no relations with any other power without consulting the Company. In signing, the head of the Maratha confederacy signed away its independence, and the other Maratha chiefs refused to accept it, which brought on the Second Anglo-Maratha War.

question: The Amara-Nayaka system was a major political innovation of which Indian imperial rulers?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Vijayanagara. The stem is the school textbook's own sentence turned into a question: the amara-nayaka system was a major political innovation of the Vijayanagara Empire. The amara-nayakas were military commanders to whom the raya assigned territories to govern. Each collected taxes and other dues from the peasants, craftspersons and traders of his area, kept a part for himself and for maintaining a stipulated contingent of horses and elephants, and spent some of the rest on temples and irrigation works. Those contingents added up to the army with which the Vijayanagara kings brought the whole southern peninsula under their control. The obligations that kept the arrangement from becoming hereditary independence were annual tribute and a personal appearance at court with gifts, and the kings occasionally reminded a nayaka of his place by transferring him elsewhere. In the seventeenth century many of them stopped appearing, set up kingdoms of their own, and the imperial structure collapsed the faster for it.

question: KIRAN (Knowledge Involvement in Research Advancement through Nurturing) is an initiative to provide opportunities to women scientists who
opt_a: had a break in their career due to family reasons.
opt_b: are pursuing innovative research in life sciences.
opt_c: have collaborative projects with labs in foreign countries.
opt_d: have leading edge projects in Nano-Science and Technology.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, had a break in their career due to family reasons. That is the defining feature of the programme, not an incidental benefit. The Department of Science and Technology describes KIRAN as aimed at women scientists and technologists aged 27 to 57 who had a break in their career , primarily on account of family responsibilities, and who wish to return to the mainstream. The design follows from the diagnosis. Indian women enter science degrees in large numbers and thin out sharply in research careers, and the point at which most drop away is marriage, childbirth and caregiving. Because the barrier is not the subject, the remedy cannot be a field-specific research grant; it has to be an age-relaxed re-entry route with a fellowship attached, which is what the Women Scientist Scheme provides.

question: NIDHI is an umbrella scheme for the promotion of
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, young and aspiring innovators. NIDHI stands for National Initiative for Developing and Harnessing Innovations, and its own portal describes it as an umbrella programme of the Department of Science and Technology for nurturing ideas and innovations, whether knowledge-based or technology-driven, into successful startups. That is the whole arc the scheme is built to carry (from a person with an idea to a company with a product) and the components are laid out along it: PRAYAS puts money and a workshop behind an early prototype, the Entrepreneur-in-Residence support carries an individual through the risky first year, Technology Business Incubators host the young firm, Seed Support funds it, and the Accelerator pushes it to market. The entry-level component even spells the answer out, since PRAYAS is the promotion of young and aspiring innovators at the prototype stage.

question: The Saubhagya Scheme aims at universal
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, household electrification. Saubhagya is short for Pradhan Mantri Sahaj Bijli Har Ghar Yojana, and the name carries the answer: sahaj bijli har ghar, easy electricity for every home. Announced in September 2017 by the Ministry of Power, it was aimed at the last mile: not at reaching villages, which earlier programmes had largely done, but at connecting the individual houses inside them that still had no meter. The distinction is the point of the scheme. A village counted as electrified once public places and a tenth of its households had power, so a village could be electrified on paper while most of its families still used kerosene. Saubhagya went after those families directly, giving free connections to households identified from the Socio-Economic and Caste Census of 2011 and charging others Rs 500, recoverable in instalments. The outlay was about Rs 16,320 crore, of which Rs 12,320 crore was gross budgetary support.

question: Mission Indradhanush aims at
opt_a: reducing child deaths due to pneumonia.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, full immunisation of children. Mission Indradhanush was launched on 25 December 2014 by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare with the stated aim of driving full immunisation coverage to 90 per cent and holding it there. The rainbow in the name is the clue to its scope: the seven colours stood for the seven vaccine-preventable diseases the universal programme then covered: diphtheria, whooping cough, tetanus, poliomyelitis, tuberculosis, measles and hepatitis B. A child is counted as fully immunised only when every due dose has been received, and the mission's method was to find the children who had been missed or only partly covered and complete their schedule, through catch-up rounds in districts with the worst records. That is why the answer has to be the general one. The three other options each name a single disease or vaccine, and a programme organised around one pathogen could not deliver a full schedule.

question: Which one of the following statements about the DDU – GKY is not correct?
opt_a: It is a skill training programme.
opt_b: It is for rural youth from poor families.
opt_c: Its objective is placement in wage employment.
opt_d: It relies entirely on skill training by Government agencies.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, It relies entirely on skill training by Government agencies. The word that fails is 'entirely' . The Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Grameen Kaushalya Yojana does not train anybody itself; it sanctions projects to Project Implementing Agencies , and those agencies are overwhelmingly outside government: companies, industry bodies, trusts and non-governmental organisations. The Ministry of Rural Development sets the rules, funds the projects and audits the outcomes; partners deliver the training against common guidelines and standard operating procedures. That structure follows from the scheme's target. At least three-quarters of those who complete training must be placed in wage employment at a stated minimum salary, and only an agency close to the employers doing the hiring can guarantee placement, which a purely governmental training system is not.

question: Which of the following statements about the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana are correct? 1. It is part of Government of India's poverty reduction strategy. 2. It is a centrally sponsored scheme for rural development. 3. It provides connectivity in rural areas. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, 1, 2 and 3. All three statements come straight out of the programme's own guidelines. On the first, the guidelines open by saying that rural road connectivity is not only a key component of rural development in India but is also recognised as an effective poverty reduction programme, and the ministry's later restatement puts it even more plainly: the Government launched the yojana as part of the poverty reduction strategy. On the second, the Prime Minister announced it on 15 August 2000 as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme, and from 2001-02 it ran as a wholly centrally sponsored one; the programme is administered by the Ministry of Rural Development. On the third, its object is road connectivity through good all-weather roads to rural habitations: originally those above 1,000 persons, then above 500 in the plains and not less than 250 in hilly and desert tracts. No statement can be dropped, so the all-of-them option is the answer.

question: India's territorial limit extends towards the sea up to
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, 12 nautical miles. The figure is fixed by statute. The Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and other Maritime Zones Act, 1976, provides in section 3 that the limit of the territorial waters is the line every point of which is at a distance of twelve nautical miles from the nearest point of the appropriate baseline. The same section declares that the sovereignty of India extends, and has always extended, to those waters and to the seabed and subsoil beneath them and the airspace above them, so this belt is not a zone of special rights but Indian territory in the full sense, subject only to the right of innocent passage that international law gives to foreign ships. The Central Government may alter the limit by notification, having regard to international law and State practice, but it has not done so. Twelve is also the maximum any coastal state may claim under the Law of the Sea Convention, which is why the figure is the same the world over.

question: Which one of the following is a cold ocean current?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, California Current. It is a cold-water Pacific current that moves southward along the western coast of North America, forming the eastern limb of the North Pacific gyre. Two features of the description settle its temperature without any memorising. It flows from higher latitudes towards the equator, so it carries cool water into warmer seas. And it runs down the eastern side of the ocean basin, where the wind pushes surface water away from the coast and colder water rises from below to replace it: the California Current is one of the world's great upwelling systems, which is why its waters are cold, nutrient-rich and among the most productive fishing grounds on earth. The same combination explains the fog that hangs over the coast in summer and the aridity of the land behind it.

question: Identify the type of soil on the basis of the given characteristics : 1. They are rich in lime, iron, magnesia and alumina. 2. They are generally clayey, deep and impermeable. 3. They are mainly found in Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat. Select the correct answer from the given alternatives :
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Black soil. All three clues are the school text's own sentences about black soil, in its own order: chemically rich in lime, iron, magnesia and alumina; generally clayey, deep and impermeable; covering most of the Deccan Plateau, including parts of Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh and some parts of Tamil Nadu. Each clue has a physical explanation. The soil forms from the weathering of Deccan basaltic lava , a lime-, iron- and magnesium-rich rock, so the chemistry is inherited from the parent material. The clay swells and becomes sticky when wet and shrinks and cracks widely when dry, so a kind of self-ploughing occurs. Because it absorbs and loses moisture slowly, it holds water long into the dry season, which is why rain-fed cotton does so well on it that it is also called black cotton soil , or regur.

question: Arabica, Robusta and Liberica are varieties of which one of the following?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Coffee. All three names belong to the genus Coffea, and the three that matter commercially are exactly these. Coffea arabica accounts for roughly 55 per cent of world coffee production and Coffea canephora, universally called Robusta, for about 45 per cent, leaving Coffea liberica as the small third species. The two leaders differ in ways worth knowing: Arabica prefers higher, cooler, shaded slopes, is more susceptible to disease, and is prized for flavour; Robusta tolerates heat and lower elevations, resists leaf rust better, carries roughly twice the caffeine and is the mainstay of instant coffee. India grows both (Karnataka is the leading producer, with Kerala and Tamil Nadu next) and its plantations are known for coffee raised under shade trees. The paper calls them varieties, which is loose in the botanist's sense since these are separate species rather than varieties within one, but the intended meaning is plain.

question: Aluminium is manufactured from
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Bauxite ore. The school text puts it exactly: though several ores contain aluminium, it is from bauxite, a clay-like substance, that alumina and later aluminium is obtained. Bauxite forms by the decomposition of a wide variety of rocks rich in aluminium silicates, under hot wet conditions that leach the silica away and leave hydrated aluminium oxides behind. Production runs in two stages: bauxite is first refined into alumina, and alumina is then reduced to the metal in an electrolytic cell, which is why aluminium smelters are built next to cheap power rather than next to mines. The metal is worth this trouble because it combines the strength of metals such as iron with extreme lightness, along with good conductivity and great malleability. In India, Odisha leads production, and the Panchpatmali deposits in Koraput district are the most important in that state.

question: Which one of the following sea ports gained significance for handling iron-ore exports to Japan?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Mormugao. It is the ore port of India, and the textbook fact behind the answer is unambiguous: Mormugao port in Goa is the premier iron-ore exporting port of the country, accounting for about fifty per cent of India's iron ore export. Geography made it so. The port occupies a naturally protected open harbour at the mouth of the Zuari estuary, and the iron and manganese fields of the Goan interior lie close behind it, so ore could move by barge down the Mandovi and Zuari and be loaded straight into bulk carriers. It became a major port in 1963, under the Major Port Trusts Act of that year, soon after Goa's incorporation into India, and it is the ore trade that gave it its standing. On the Japan connection specifically, the textbooks of this period tie the port's rise to long-term ore contracts with Japanese steel mills; that destination could not be confirmed here from a primary or reference source, so treat the port's identity as the examinable fact and the buyer as period colour. The buyer has in any case moved: of the roughly 54.5 million tonnes of iron-ore traffic Mormugao handled in 2010-11, about 90 per cent went to China.

question: Which one of the following is not a function of money?
opt_a: Acts as an intermediate in the exchange process
opt_b: Acts as a store of value
opt_c: Used as the unit of account
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Used for regulating consumption. The other three are the textbook functions of money and this one is not on the list. Money's first and foremost role is that it acts as a medium of exchange, which is what removes the double coincidence of wants that makes barter so difficult: the rice-grower no longer has to find a cloth-seller who happens to want rice. Money also acts as a convenient unit of account, because the value of all goods and services can be expressed in monetary units and relative prices can then be calculated from them. And money can act as a store of value, because unlike rice it does not perish, is cheap to store and is acceptable to anyone at any time, so wealth can be carried forward for future use. Regulating consumption is not a property of money at all; it is something a government may try to do with taxes, subsidies, rationing or credit rules, and money is merely the medium through which those measures work.

question: The situation where the equilibrium level of real GDP falls short of potential GDP is known as
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Recessionary gap. The stem sets two quantities against each other, the level of real GDP the economy actually settles at and the potential GDP it would produce with its resources fully employed, and names the case where the first is below the second. That shortfall is the recessionary gap , also called a deflationary gap. With output below capacity there is unused plant and unemployed labour, so demand is deficient and prices are under downward rather than upward pressure. Since the shortfall is one of aggregate demand, the standard remedy is expansionary policy : more government spending, lower taxes, easier credit. Question 1 of this paper defines potential GDP, so the two items are two halves of one idea.

question: The excess of total expenditure of Government over its total receipts, excluding borrowings, is known as
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, fiscal deficit. The stem is the standard definition almost word for word: fiscal deficit is the difference between the government's total expenditure and its total receipts excluding borrowing. Written out, the gross fiscal deficit equals total expenditure minus revenue receipts and non-debt creating capital receipts , such as recoveries of loans and proceeds from the sale of public sector undertakings. The words 'excluding borrowings' are the point of the measure. If borrowing counted as a receipt the books would always balance, because a government borrows whatever it does not otherwise fund. Leaving borrowing out turns the number into the government's total borrowing requirement, which from the financing side equals net borrowing at home plus borrowing from the Reserve Bank plus borrowing from abroad.

question: Exchange rates state the value of one currency in terms of other currencies. Which one of the following statements with respect to the exchange rate of currency is correct ?
opt_a: Floating exchange rates are rates in which the Governments interfere by buying or selling their currencies.
opt_b: Fixed exchange rates are rates set by Government decisions and maintained by Government actions.
opt_c: Under the Bretton Woods System, the exchange rates are floated in terms of rise or fall in price of gold.
opt_d: Under the classical gold standard, the exchange rates are fixed in terms of price of dollar.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Fixed exchange rates are rates set by Government decisions and maintained by Government actions. Both halves are right, and the second is the one candidates forget. In a fixed exchange rate system the government fixes the rate at a particular level, but fixing a price does not make the market clear at it. If the announced rate leaves an excess supply of foreign currency the authorities must buy the surplus; if it leaves an excess demand they must sell foreign currency out of their reserves, and if they cannot, a black market appears. So a fixed rate is maintained by continuous official action , and it survives only as long as the market believes the reserves are sufficient. Where that belief fails, aggressive selling of the currency forces a devaluation , the pattern seen before the collapse of the Bretton Woods system.

question: François Bernier was physician to
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Prince Dara Shikoh. The school text is explicit: Bernier was in India for twelve years, from 1656 to 1668, and was closely associated with the Mughal court as a physician to Prince Dara Shukoh, the eldest son of Emperor Shah Jahan, and later as an intellectual and scientist with Danishmand Khan, an Armenian noble at the court. The dates explain why the association was short. Bernier reached India in 1656 and the war of succession broke out the next year; Dara Shukoh was defeated and executed in 1659, after which Bernier attached himself to Danishmand Khan and stayed until 1668. He was a Frenchman who was doctor, political philosopher and historian at once, and the book that came out of these years, dedicated to Louis XIV, is the source of the argument that there was no private property in land in the Mughal Empire and that this explained everything he thought was wrong with it. The claim is disputed by historians, but it shaped European writing on Asia for a century.

question: Which one of the following British firms was taken over by Soorajmull-Nagarmull group?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, McLeod. Around 1952-53, companies fronting for the Surajmull Nagarmull group bought up the jute companies under the control of McLeod and Company , which at the time managed and owned ten jute mills, sixteen tea companies and light railways. Founded by Charles McLeod in the 1880s as a Calcutta jute trading firm, McLeod had grown into one of the great managing agencies; it passed to C. L. Bajoria of the Surajmull Nagarmull house. The group was a partnership of two Marwari families of Calcutta related by marriage, those of Surajmull Jalan and Nagarmull Bajoria, traders in the 1930s who moved into jute manufacturing in the 1940s. This takeover turned them into a conglomerate, and the group is one of the two Calcutta houses that rose almost entirely on the purchase of British firms.

question: Which one of the following statements with regard to ryotwari settlement is not correct?
opt_a: In southern and western India, the ryotwari settlement was adopted.
opt_b: Ryotwari was in principle a direct contract between the ryot and the state.
opt_c: It means a tax contract valid for usually 30 years.
opt_d: In principle, it strengthened the former elite, the zamindars and weakened the peasantry.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, In principle, it strengthened the former elite, the zamindars and weakened the peasantry. This reverses the whole design of the system, which was built to cut the intermediary out . Under ryotwari the Company assessed and taxed each individual cultivator directly, issued him a patta in his own name, and dealt with no landlord in between. That is precisely what the Permanent Settlement of Bengal (1793) did not do. It recognised zamindars as proprietors and made them the revenue-paying class; ryotwari was the alternative adopted where the Company either found no comparable landlord class or chose not to create one. The statement describes the Bengal model and attaches it to the wrong system.

question: Which one of the following statements about the British Indian Medical Service (IMS) is not correct?
opt_b: It recruited health professionals by means of a competitive examination.
opt_c: Indians were never admitted to IMS.
opt_d: The IMS was at first meant to look after the troops.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Indians were never admitted to IMS. One name settles it. Soorjo Coomar Goodeve Chuckerbutty went to London in 1854, the year the Company opened the covenanted medical examination to all candidates, and passed it in January 1855: the first Indian to do so, placing second in the list behind George Marr. He was appointed Assistant Surgeon in the covenanted service, and Rajendra Chandra Chandra followed on 27 January 1858. Indians remained a small minority in the IMS for decades, and the service was dominated by British officers to the end, but 'never admitted' is a claim that one documented entry in 1855 destroys.

question: When was the monopoly of China trade lost by East India Company?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, 1833. The Company lost its Indian trade monopoly and its China monopoly at two different moments, twenty years apart, and the question is aimed straight at that gap. The Charter Act of 1813 ended the monopoly of trade with India but expressly kept two things back for the Company: the tea trade and the trade with China. The Charter Act of 1833 finished the job: it wound up the Company's commercial business altogether, including the remaining monopoly over tea and over trade with China, and left the Company as a purely administrative body holding India in trust for the Crown. That is why 1833 is also the Act that renamed the Governor-General of Bengal as Governor-General of India and gave his Council exclusive legislative power.

question: National Disaster Management Authority is headed by
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, the Prime Minister. The Disaster Management Act, 2005 says it in terms. Section 3(2) provides that the National Authority shall consist of a Chairperson and not more than nine other members, and that unless the rules otherwise provide it shall consist of '(a) the Prime Minister of India, who shall be the Chairperson of the National Authority, ex officio; (b) other members, not exceeding nine, to be nominated by the Chairperson'. The Chairperson may designate one of the nominated members as Vice-Chairperson, who runs the Authority day to day and presides when the Prime Minister cannot attend. So the Prime Minister heads it by force of statute , not by convention.

question: Which of the following statements regarding the ‘casting vote’ in the Parliament is/are correct? 1. It is cast by the speaker or a person acting as such. 2. It is cast in addition to voting in the first instance. 3. It is cast in the case of equality of votes. 4. It is always cast to maintain the status quo. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, 1 and 3 only. Article 100(1) of the Constitution settles both halves in one sentence: 'The Chairman or Speaker, or person acting as such, shall not vote in the first instance, but shall have and exercise a casting vote in the case of an equality of votes.' Statement 1 is right, and the Article deliberately covers 'a person acting as such': the Deputy Speaker in the chair, or a member from the panel of chairpersons, exercises the same power. Statement 3 is right and names the only trigger: the vote must be tied. Statement 2 states the exact opposite of Article 100(1): the presiding officer does not vote in the first instance, so the casting vote is a substitute for that ordinary vote, not an addition to it. Statement 4 fails on 'always': preserving the status quo is a well-established convention, not a constitutional command.

question: Equality before the law or equal protection of the laws within the territory of India is guaranteed under which one of the following Articles of the Constitution of India?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Article 14. The stem is almost the text itself: 'The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.' Two distinct guarantees sit in that one line. Equality before the law is the English common-law idea, negative in form: no one is above the law, and there are no special privileges. Equal protection of the laws is drawn from the Fourteenth Amendment of the United States Constitution and is positive: like should be treated alike, which permits reasonable classification but forbids class legislation. Note also the word 'person': Article 14 protects citizens and non-citizens alike, and companies too, unlike Article 15 or Article 16, which are confined to citizens.

question: 'Legal Positivism' theory was developed by
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, John Austin. Austin, the first Professor of Jurisprudence at University College London from 1827, was the first legal thinker to work out a fully developed positivistic theory of law, and he did it in The Province of Jurisprudence Determined (1832). His command theory holds that laws are general commands issued by a sovereign to the members of an independent political society and backed by credible threats of punishment. What makes it positivism is the separation it insists on: law is a social fact, a matter of who in fact holds power and who in fact obeys, and whether a law is just is a separate question from whether it is law. The verb in the stem, 'developed by', matters: the ideas were in the air before him, and Austin is the one who systematised them.

question: Who among the following said that Democracy means a system of 'Government by Consent'?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, John Locke. Consent is the hinge of Locke's whole argument in the Second Treatise of Government (1689). Men are by nature free, equal and independent, and no one can be taken out of that condition and placed under the political power of another without his own consent. Government therefore arises when free individuals agree to leave the state of nature and entrust power to a common authority for the preservation of their lives, liberties and estates. Because the authority is held on trust , it lasts only while the trust is kept: a government that turns against the ends for which it was created forfeits its title, and the people may resume the power they gave. That is why 'government by consent' is the usual summary of Locke's account of legitimate rule, and why his argument became the standard justification for limited government and the right of resistance.

question: Milpa and Ladang are different names for
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, shifting cultivation. Both words are local names for the same practice on opposite sides of the world. Milpa is the maize-beans-squash field system of Mesoamerica, used especially in the Yucatán Peninsula of Mexico, and it runs on a swidden cycle: roughly two years of cropping followed by about eight years of fallow while the forest grows back. Ladang is the Malay and Indonesian word for a dry, unirrigated field, the counterpart of the sawah or irrigated wet-rice paddy, and it names the slash-and-burn cultivation of Malaysia and Indonesia. Clear a patch, burn the felled vegetation so the ash returns potash to the soil, crop it for a year or three until yields fall, then abandon it and move on: that single description covers both.

question: Which one of the following approaches of human development was initially proposed by the International Labour Organisation (ILO) and emphasised on health, education, food, water supply, sanitation and housing?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Basic needs approach. The stem is lifted almost word for word from the NCERT table of approaches to human development: 'This approach was initially proposed by the International Labour Organisation (ILO). Six basic needs i.e.: health, education, food, water supply, sanitation, and housing were identified. The question of human choices is ignored and the emphasis is on the provision of basic needs of defined sections.' Two markers in the stem point only one way: the ILO as the proposing body, and the six needs listed in that exact order. The approach's philosophical signature is in the last clause: it asks what people must be supplied with, and does not ask what they would choose. That is what separates it from Amartya Sen's capability approach .

question: Which one of the following tributaries of river Indus feeds the canal system of the Bhakra Nangal Project?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Satluj. Bhakra is a concrete gravity dam on the Satluj at Bhakra village, where the river leaves the Shivaliks near Bilaspur in Himachal Pradesh, and the project takes its name from Bhakra plus Nangal, the barrage about ten kilometres downstream. The canal system is fed from Nangal : water released there enters the Nangal Hydel Channel, which generates power at Ganguwal and Kotla and then feeds the Bhakra Main Line and its distributaries. The Bhakra canals irrigate about ten million acres in Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan. The Satluj is also the right answer on treaty grounds: it is one of the three eastern rivers whose waters were allocated to India under the Indus Waters Treaty of 1960, which is what made a project on this scale possible.

question: When the rivers discharge their waters from all directions into a lake or depression, the pattern is known as
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Centripetal. The stem is the NCERT definition almost unaltered: 'When the rivers discharge their waters from all directions in a lake or depression, the pattern is know as centripetal'. The school text prints 'in' where the paper prints 'into', and carries its own typographical slip in 'is know as'. The name gives the mechanism: centripetal means centre-seeking, so the streams converge inward on a low point instead of spreading outward. The landform that produces it is an enclosed basin with no outlet to the sea, such as a crater, a caldera, a structural depression or a rift-floor lake. The drainage of the Loktak lake basin in Manipur and of the inland basins of Rajasthan and of Central Asia are the standard illustrations.

question: Which one of the following statements about the Coriolis force is not correct?
opt_a: It is maximum at the Poles.
opt_b: It is absent at the Equator.
opt_c: It deflects the wind to the right direction in the southern hemisphere.
opt_d: It deflects the wind to the right direction in the northern hemisphere.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, It deflects the wind to the right direction in the southern hemisphere. The deflection reverses across the equator , and the paper has simply repeated the northern-hemisphere clause with the wrong hemisphere attached. The school text is explicit: the force 'deflects the wind to the right direction in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern hemisphere'. The other three options are that same passage broken into pieces. 'The Coriolis force is directly proportional to the angle of latitude. It is maximum at the poles and is absent at the equator' gives options (a) and (b) word for word, and the northern-hemisphere half of the deflection sentence gives option (d). Only option (c) has been altered, and the alteration is the tested point.

question: Chronologically arrange the following treaties/conventions signed between the Marathas and the British (starting with the earliest) : 1. Treaty of Salbai 2. Treaty of Purandar 3. Convention of Wadgaon 4. Treaty of Surat Select the correct answer using the code given below :
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, 4-2-3-1. All four documents belong to the First Anglo-Maratha War , and they run Surat, Purandar, Wadgaon, Salbai. The Treaty of Surat, 6 March 1775, is the war's cause: the claimant Raghunathrao bought Bombay's military support by ceding Salsette and Bassein. The Treaty of Purandar, 1 March 1776, is Calcutta overruling Bombay: the Supreme Council annulled Surat, dropped Raghunathrao and recognised the infant Madhavrao II, while keeping Salsette. The Convention of Wadgaon, 16 January 1779, is the humiliation: a British force marching on Poona was surrounded and signed a capitulation, which Warren Hastings promptly repudiated as made without authority. The Treaty of Salbai , 17 May 1782, closes the war on terms close to the status quo, confirming Madhavrao II as Peshwa.

question: Which of the following statements about the Sanyasi and Faqir disturbances/rebellions are correct? 1. Governor-General Warren Hastings faced the persistent Sanyasi and Faqir disturbances in Bengal and Bihar. 2. There were a number of Shaivite Naga Sanyasis who formed into armed bands. 3. Majnu Shah, who led bands into Bengal from 1771, was their prominent leader. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, 1, 2 and 3. All three statements stand. Statement 1: the disturbances ran from about 1763 to 1800 across Bengal and Bihar, so they span exactly the years Warren Hastings governed (Governor of Bengal from 1772, Governor-General from 1774). Suppressing them was one of the standing problems of his administration. Statement 2: the sanyasi side was made up of Dasnami Naga ascetics, an order in the Shaivite tradition whose akharas were organised on military lines and who moved in armed bands. Statement 3: the faqir side was led by Majnu Shah, a Madari faqir who led bands into Bengal from 1771 and remained their most prominent leader until the late 1780s.

question: In 1943, young leaders in which one of the following districts of Maharashtra set up a parallel Government (prati sarkar) with volunteer corps (seva dals) and village units (tufan dals)?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Satara. The Satara prati sarkar is the longest-lived of the parallel governments thrown up by the Quit India Movement. It was led by Krantisinh Nana Patil , who spent forty-four months underground after 1942. The Ballia rising lasted weeks, and the Tamluk Jatiya Sarkar in Midnapore lasted until Gandhi asked its leaders to disband in 1944. The Satara administration ran on into the mid-1940s, holding its own courts, settling disputes, organising grain supply and running a village-based armed volunteer network of the kind the question describes. Its recruits were largely young men from the district's peasant families, which is why the paper speaks of 'young leaders' rather than of the established Congress leadership.

question: Who founded the Central Hindu School at Benaras which was later developed into Benaras Hindu University?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Annie Besant. Besant founded the school at Benaras in July 1898, with Dr Arthur Richardson, a science graduate from England, as its first principal. Her purpose was a school that would teach Western science and English alongside Hindu religious instruction, in keeping with the Theosophical Society 's programme of reviving Indian traditions rather than displacing them. She later dedicated the institution to Madan Mohan Malaviya, and it became the nucleus of Banaras Hindu University when the University was established in 1916. Besant built the school and Malaviya built the University on it; the paper is testing whether a candidate can keep the two acts apart.

question: Which one among the following is not a feature of centralization?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Liberty. Liberty is the standing argument for decentralisation , not a claim made for centralisation. The case for concentrating authority at a single centre has always rested on unity, uniformity of law and administration, speed of decision and economies of scale. The other three options are the standard textbook merits of centralisation. The case against it, from Tocqueville and Mill onwards, is that liberty needs distance and plurality : many centres of power that check one another, local bodies in which ordinary citizens learn self-government, and decisions taken close enough to the governed to be answerable to them. Concentrating power in one authority removes exactly those safeguards.

question: Which one of the following is not an objective of NITI Aayog?
opt_a: It provides a critical direction and strategic input for development process.
opt_b: It functions as a 'think tank' in providing key elements of policy.
opt_c: It monitors and evaluates the implementation of the programmes.
opt_d: It offers a platform for resolution of inter-state conflicts as 'provider of first and last resort'.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, It offers a platform for resolution of inter-state conflicts as 'provider of first and last resort'. NITI Aayog's own statement of objectives does contain a clause about a platform for resolution, but of a different kind of dispute: 'To offer a platform for the resolution of inter-sectoral and inter-departmental issues in order to accelerate the implementation of the development agenda.' Inter-sectoral and inter-departmental issues mean friction between ministries and between sectors of policy. The option quietly changes it to inter-state , a constitutional function that belongs elsewhere: to the Inter-State Council under Article 263 for general disputes, and to tribunals under the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 for river waters. The quoted phrase 'provider of first and last resort' does not appear anywhere in NITI Aayog's stated objectives either.

question: Article 231 of the Constitution of India grants power to establish a common High Court for two or more states to
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, the Parliament. Article 231(1) reads: 'Parliament may by law establish a common High Court for two or more States or for two or more States and a Union territory.' The two operative words are Parliament and by law : this is legislative power, exercised through a statute, not an executive act of the President or an order of any court. Several High Courts have exactly this character: the Gauhati High Court has served a group of north-eastern States, the Punjab and Haryana High Court serves two States and the Union Territory of Chandigarh, and the Bombay and Madras High Courts extend to Union Territories. Article 231 also settles the consequential questions, applying the references to the Governor, the State Public Service Commission and the State Legislature in the judges' provisions to each of the States concerned.

question: Which one among the following motions cannot be made while introducing an ordinary Bill in the Parliament?
opt_a: That the Bill be taken into consideration
opt_b: That the Bill be circulated for the purpose of eliciting public opinion
opt_c: That the Bill be referred to a Select Committee
opt_d: That the Bill be referred to a Joint Committee of the House without the concurrence of the other House
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, That the Bill be referred to a Joint Committee of the House without the concurrence of the other House. The whole option turns on its last five words. Once a Bill has been introduced and published, the member in charge may move that it be taken into consideration, referred to a Select Committee of that House, circulated for eliciting opinion, or referred to a Joint Committee of the Houses. But a Joint Committee, by definition, is drawn from both Houses, and one House cannot conscript members of the other. So a reference to a Joint Committee is made by a motion in one House which is transmitted to the other for its agreement, and the committee is constituted only when the second House concurs . Strip the concurrence away and the motion becomes something the House has no power to make.

question: Which one among the following was eliminated by the 44th Amendment Act of the Parliament?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Right to Property. The Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, passed by the Janata government after the Emergency, omitted Article 19(1)(f) (the freedom 'to acquire, hold and dispose of property') and repealed Article 31. In their place it inserted Article 300A in Part XII: 'No person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.' The deletion is visible in the text to this day: Article 19(1) now runs (a), (b), (c), (d), (e) and (g), skipping (f) altogether. Property thus ceased to be a Fundamental Right and became a constitutional or legal right. It can no longer be enforced by moving the Supreme Court directly under Article 32, and because Article 300A says 'person' rather than 'citizen', it now protects non-citizens and companies as well.

question: Identify the crop on the basis of the following characteristics: 1. It is a kharif crop. 2. Aus, Aman and Boro are its three different growing periods in an agricultural year. 3. About one-fourth of the total cropped area of India is under its cultivation. Select the correct answer using the code given below.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Rice. Each of the three clues is a sentence from the school geography text on rice. Aus, aman and boro are the three crops of rice grown in West Bengal in one agricultural year, so clue 2 identifies the crop on its own: no other Indian crop carries those names. Clue 3 matches the textbook figure that about one-fourth of the total cropped area is under rice, far ahead of pulses at about eleven per cent and cotton at about 4.7 per cent. Clue 1 fits too: in the Himalayas and the north-western parts of the country rice is grown as a kharif crop during the south-west monsoon. Where the eastern and southern regions have enough rainfall or irrigation, two or three crops of rice are taken in a year, which is what the aus-aman-boro cycle records.

question: Which one of the following is a type of igneous rock?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Granite. Granite forms when magma cools slowly deep inside the crust, which gives its crystals of quartz, feldspar and mica time to grow large enough to be seen with the naked eye. That coarse-grained texture marks a plutonic or intrusive igneous rock . Basalt is its extrusive counterpart: the same broad family of melt, cooled fast at the surface and therefore fine-grained, as in the Deccan Traps. The other three options cover the remaining ways a rock can form without ever having been molten: marble is metamorphic, and halite and shale are sedimentary.

question: Ozone layer, which absorbs the ultra-violet radiation, is found in which one of the following layers of the atmosphere?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Stratosphere. The ozone layer sits in the lower and middle stratosphere , roughly fifteen to thirty-five kilometres up, where it absorbs essentially all incoming UV-C and most UV-B. That absorption is what creates the layer's structure. Because ozone converts ultraviolet energy into heat, temperature rises with height through the stratosphere instead of falling, and that inversion makes the layer stable, free of vertical convection and almost cloudless. The same stability is why jet aircraft cruise in the lower stratosphere.

question: Which one of the following statements about primary waves of earthquakes is not correct?
opt_a: They are similar to sound waves.
opt_b: They can travel only through solid materials.
opt_c: They travel through gaseous, liquid and solid materials.
opt_d: They move faster and are the first to arrive at the surface.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, They can travel only through solid materials. That is the defining property of the S-wave, not the P-wave, and the paper has simply moved it across. The school text is unambiguous on both: 'P-waves move faster and are the first to arrive at the surface. These are also called primary waves. The P-waves are similar to sound waves. They travel through gaseous, liquid and solid materials' (which is options (d), (a) and (c) word for word) and then, of the secondary wave, 'an important fact about S-waves is that they can travel only through solid materials'. The physics behind the difference is that a P-wave is a compressional wave, vibrating parallel to its direction of travel, and any material can be compressed; an S-wave is a shear wave, vibrating across its direction of travel, and fluids have no rigidity to resist shear. Note also that options (b) and (c) contradict each other outright, which by itself tells a careful reader that one of them must be the answer.

question: Alluvial soils vary in nature from sandy loam to clay. They are generally
opt_a: poor in potash and rich in phosphorus.
opt_b: poor in both potash and phosphorus.
opt_c: rich in both potash and phosphorus.
opt_d: rich in potash and poor in phosphorus.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, rich in potash and poor in phosphorus. The whole question is a single sentence lifted from the school geography chapter on soils: 'The alluvial soils vary in nature from sandy loam to clay. They are generally rich in potash but poor in phosphorous .' The paper has put the first part in the stem and made the second part the answer. The four options are simply the four ways of pairing rich and poor with the two nutrients, and only one of them restores the original line. Alluvial soils are India's most extensive and most productive group, and their fertility comes from constant renewal by river deposition rather than from any one nutrient.

question: Who among the following was popularly known as 'Lokahitwadi'?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Gopal Hari Deshmukh. Lokahitwadi was not a title conferred on him but a pen-name he chose: lokhit means the public good in Marathi, and he began signing his reform writings with it at the age of twenty-five, in the Marathi weekly Prabhakar. Within about two years he had written more than a hundred such pieces, collected and remembered as the Shatapatre, the hundred letters. Their subjects are the standard programme of nineteenth-century western Indian reform: the emancipation of women, opposition to child marriage, dowry and polygamy, and an attack on caste privilege, including the claim of Brahmin superiority made from within a Brahmin household. The pen-name stuck so completely that he is better known by it than by his given name.

question: Who among the following socialist activists persuaded Gandhiji not to restrict the salt march protest to men alone?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay. The stem is taken almost word for word from the school history chapter on Gandhi, which says of the Salt March that 'it was the first nationalist activity in which women participated in large numbers. The socialist activist Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay had persuaded Gandhiji not to restrict the protests to men alone.' Even the phrase 'socialist activist' comes from that sentence, and it is the surest signal in the item: of the four women, she is the one the text identifies by a political affiliation rather than by a role in the Congress. Kamaladevi herself courted arrest by breaking the salt or liquor laws, was named to the seven-member team Gandhi announced for making salt at the Bombay beachfront, and later became the moving force behind the revival of Indian handicrafts and handloom.

question: Which one of the following painters was not associated with Humayun?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Bihzad. Kamal ud-Din Bihzad , who lived from about 1455 to 1535, was the supreme master of the Persian miniature, and he never came to India . He worked at Herat under the Timurid Sultan Husayn Bayqara, passed into Safavid service under Shah Ismail I in 1522 and then under Shah Tahmasp I, and died in 1535, when Humayun was still fighting Bahadur Shah of Gujarat and more than a decade before Humayun's own painters joined him. Mughal emperors paid large sums for his paintings, but that is collecting at a distance, not employment. The other three names are the ones the official answer treats as Humayun's.

question: Match List I with List II and select the correct answer using the code given below the lists: List I (Author) A. Brindavan Das B. Krishnadas Kaviraj C. Mukundaram Chakravarti D. Rameshwar Bhattacharya List II (Poetical work) 1. Shivasankirttan 2. Chandimangal 3. Chaitanyacharitamrita 4. Chaitanyamangal
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, 4 3 2 1. Take the two Chaitanya biographies first, because they decide the answer. Krishnadas Kaviraj , who settled at Vrindavan and wrote in old age with a trembling hand, produced the Chaitanyacharitamrita , so B goes to 3. That leaves Chaitanyamangal for Brindavan Das. His life of Chaitanya was first called Chaitanya Mangala, and the Vaishnava elders renamed it Chaitanya Bhagavata only after they found that Lochan Das had already published a book under that title. Mukundaram Chakravarti, the poet of Daminya in Bardhaman who wrote as Kabikankan, is the author of the Chandimangal, the great mangal-kavya of the goddess Chandi, so C goes to 2. Rameshwar Bhattacharya is left with Shivasankirttan, the early-eighteenth-century Bengali poem on Shiva. Reading down: A-4, B-3, C-2, D-1.

question: Which one of the following scholars of Akbar's court translated Bhaskaracharya's Lilavati into Persian?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Faizi. Abu al-Faiz ibn Mubarak, known as Faizi, rendered the Lilavati into Persian around 1587. He was the elder brother of Abul Fazl, tutor to Akbar's sons, sadr of several regions from 1581 and poet laureate of the court from 1588, and he also turned the Yogavasistha into Persian and wrote the romance Nal o Daman before his death at Lahore on 15 October 1595. The Lilavati is the arithmetic book of the Siddhanta Shiromani, the twelfth-century treatise of Bhaskara II, and its 277 verses on measurement, progressions and permutations were exactly the kind of practical Sanskrit learning Akbar's translation programme wanted in Persian.

question: Who among the following was the Chairman of the National Commission for Review of the Working of the Constitution (2000)?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Justice M.N. Venkatachaliah. The National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution was set up in February 2000 under the chairmanship of Venkatachaliah, who had been Chief Justice of India in 1993-94. Its eleven members included B.P. Jeevan Reddy, R.S. Sarkaria, Soli Sorabjee, K. Parasaran, Subhash C. Kashyap and P.A. Sangma, and it delivered a report of about 1,979 pages in two volumes on 31 March 2002. Its brief was deliberately narrow: to examine how the Constitution had worked in practice within the framework of parliamentary democracy, without disturbing the basic structure.

question: M.M. Punchhi Commission on Centre-State Relations has recommended the disposal of a bill reserved for the consideration of the Union Executive within
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, six months. The Punchhi Commission's reasoning is set out in Volume II of its report and repeated in its summary of recommendations. Article 201 already binds the State Legislature to a six-month limit for reconsidering a Bill that the President has returned with a message, while nothing at all binds the President. A reserved Bill can therefore be held back indefinitely: in the Commission's words, retained at the Central level even beyond the life of the State Legislature. Its recommendation is that the same six-month period in Article 201 be made applicable to the President for deciding whether to assent to or withhold assent from a reserved Bill. It recommended six months for the Governor's own decision as well.

question: Who among the following founded the Marathi newspaper 'Kesari'?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Lokmanya Tilak. Bal Gangadhar Tilak started two weeklies together on 4 January 1881 (Kesari in Marathi and Mahratta in English) and used the Marathi paper to reach an audience that the English press could not touch. Kesari carried the writing that twice took him to prison for sedition, including the articles after the killing of Rand in 1897 and the pieces of 1908 that earned him six years in Mandalay. Both papers are still brought out by the Kesari Mahratta Trust in Pune.

question: Which mega public sector undertaking is designated with 'Navratna' status?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Bharat Electronics Limited. BEL is the only one of the four that sits on the Navratna list. Indian Oil, GAIL and Bharat Petroleum are all on the Maharatna list, which is the tier above: a Maharatna board may commit up to about 5,000 crore rupees to a single project without going back to the government, a Navratna board up to about 1,000 crore. BEL is a Ministry of Defence company headquartered in Bengaluru, making radars, avionics, weapon systems, communication equipment and the electronic voting machines used in Indian elections, and it was the first defence public sector undertaking to reach Mini Ratna Category-I, in 2002, before its Navratna grant.

question: Which of the following statements with regard to the creation of a new state or alteration of boundaries of states is/are correct? 1. An amendment has to be moved in the Parliament under Article 368 of the Constitution of India. 2. Ratification by one half of the states is necessary after the amendment is made by the Parliament. 3. The legislation can be passed by a simple majority of both Houses of Parliament. Select the correct answer using the code given below.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, 3 only. Creating a State is done under Article 3, not Article 368, and it is done by an ordinary law. Article 3 lets Parliament form a new State, increase or diminish the area of a State, alter its boundaries or change its name; the only extra requirement is procedural: the Bill needs the President's recommendation and must first be referred to the legislature of the affected State for its views, which Parliament is free to ignore once the time allowed has run out. Such a law does amend the First and Fourth Schedules, but Article 4(2) settles the point in terms: no such law shall be deemed to be an amendment of this Constitution for the purposes of Article 368. So no special majority, and no ratification by the States. Only statement 3 survives.

question: Which one of the following is the largest linguistic group of India?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Indo-Aryan. The 2011 Census puts about 78 per cent of Indians in the Indo-Aryan group (the Indo-European total is 945,333,910 speakers, or 78.07 per cent) and no other family comes close. Dravidian is second with 237,840,116 speakers, 19.64 per cent. Austroasiatic, which older Indian textbooks call Austric, accounts for 13,493,080 speakers or 1.11 per cent, and Sino-Tibetan for 12,257,382, almost exactly 1 per cent. Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Gujarati, Punjabi, Odia, Assamese, Kashmiri, Sindhi, Nepali and Urdu are all Indo-Aryan, which is why the total is so large.

question: Which one of the following water bodies separates the Andaman and the Nicobar islands?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Ten Degree Channel. The channel runs along roughly the tenth parallel of north latitude, is about 150 km wide, and separates Little Andaman at the southern end of the Andaman group from Car Nicobar at the northern end of the Nicobar group. It is the break in the archipelago, and a busy shipping lane between the Bay of Bengal and the Strait of Malacca. Going north to south the chain reads North Andaman with Saddle Peak, Middle Andaman, South Andaman with Port Blair, then Duncan Passage, Little Andaman, the Ten Degree Channel, Car Nicobar, the central Nicobars and Great Nicobar, which ends at Indira Point.

question: Which one of the following longitudes is the standard meridian of India?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, 82°30' E. India keeps a single clock set to the local mean time of 82 degrees 30 minutes east longitude, a line that passes near Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh. The arithmetic is fixed: the Earth turns 360 degrees in 24 hours, so 15 degrees of longitude is one hour and 82.5 divided by 15 gives 5.5: Indian Standard Time is therefore UTC plus five and a half hours. The two western options can be dismissed without any calculation, since the whole of India lies east of Greenwich, between roughly 68 and 97 degrees east.

question: Match List I with List II and select the correct answer using the code given below the lists: List I (Tropical Cyclones) A. Cyclones B. Hurricanes C. Typhoons D. Willy-willies List II (Region) 1. Western Australia 2. South China Sea 3. Indian Ocean 4. Atlantic Ocean Code:
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, 3, 4, 2, 1. The four names in List I are regional labels for one and the same storm (a tropical cyclone) and each belongs to the ocean where it was coined. Cyclone is the Indian Ocean word, so A goes to 3. Hurricane belongs to the Atlantic and the eastern Pacific, giving B to 4. Typhoon is the western Pacific and South China Sea word, so C goes to 2. Willy-willy is the Australian term, which leaves D with 1, Western Australia. Reading across, A-3, B-4, C-2, D-1.

question: Which of the following is/are social security scheme(s)? 1. Atal Pension Yojana 2. Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana 3. Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana Select the correct answer using the code given below:
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, 1, 2 and 3. All three belong to the Jan Suraksha package announced in the 2015 budget and launched together that May, and all three are social security schemes in the ordinary sense of pooling small contributions against old age, death or disability. Atal Pension Yojana is a guaranteed pension for unorganised sector workers, paying between 1,000 and 5,000 rupees a month from the age of 60 depending on what the subscriber chose and when he joined. Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana is a one-year renewable life cover of two lakh rupees for account holders aged 18 to 50. Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana is accident insurance, two lakh rupees for accidental death or total disability and one lakh for partial disability, for account holders aged 18 to 70.

question: Which one of the following units is not a part of All India Radio’s Transcription and Programme Exchange Service?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Advanced Research Unit. Prasar Bharati's own account of its archives names the working parts, and an advanced research unit is not among them. The Central Archives in New Delhi runs through two wings, the All India Radio Archives and the Doordarshan Archives, and holds something like 47,000 magnetic tapes. Within it sit a sound archive of recordings and spoken word material, a transcription service whose job is to transcribe and preserve recordings of speeches by Presidents and Prime Ministers, a programme exchange unit that circulates serials, features, community songs, dramas and monthly chain plays among stations across the country, and support units for refurbishing old recordings and for commercial release. Research on broadcasting is done elsewhere in Prasar Bharati, not as a limb of this service.

question: Which of the following statements about the Panchayati Raj System are correct? 1. All seats in a Panchayat are filled by persons chosen by direct election. 2. The ‘Gram Sabha’ consists of persons registered in the village electoral rolls. 3. The Chairperson of a Panchayat is elected in accordance with a law passed by each state. 4. All states in India have a three-tier system of Panchayats. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, 1, 2 and 3 only. Statement 1 restates Article 243C(2) almost word for word: all the seats in a Panchayat shall be filled by persons chosen by direct election from territorial constituencies in the Panchayat area. Statement 2 is the definition in Article 243(b), which says a Gram Sabha is a body consisting of persons registered in the electoral rolls relating to a village. Statement 3 follows Article 243C(5)(a), under which the chairperson of a village Panchayat is elected in such manner as the legislature of the State may provide. Statement 4 is the one that fails. Article 243B(1) does require Panchayats at village, intermediate and district levels, but clause (2) adds that the intermediate level may be left out in a State whose population does not exceed twenty lakh, so the three-tier system is not universal.

question: Which of the following statements is/are correct? 1. The elections to the Panchayat are conducted by the State Election Commission. 2. The State Election Commissioner is appointed by the Chief Election Commissioner of India. 3. The State Legislatures have the power to make laws on all matters relating to Panchayat elections. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, 1 and 3 only. Statement 1 is Article 243K(1), which vests the superintendence, direction and control of Panchayat elections, and of the preparation of electoral rolls for them, in a State Election Commission. Statement 3 is Article 243K(4), which lets the legislature of a State make provision, subject to the Constitution, with respect to all matters relating to or in connection with elections to the Panchayats. Statement 2 is the one that fails, and it fails on the appointing authority: the same clause 243K(1) says the State Election Commissioner is appointed by the Governor. The Chief Election Commissioner of India has no role at all in the State Election Commission: the two bodies are constitutionally separate.

question: Which one of the following is not a correct description of the Union Cabinet?
opt_a: It is part of the Parliament.
opt_b: It is responsible to the Parliament.
opt_c: It remains in power till it enjoys the confidence of the Parliament.
opt_d: A person from outside the Parliament can never be appointed a member of the Cabinet.
source_answer_raw: This question was cancelled by the commission (marks awarded to all).
source_explanation_raw: UPSC dropped this question from the paper. No option is keyed and no candidate gained or lost a mark on it. The stem asks which statement is not a correct description of the Union Cabinet, and two of the four are wrong, so the item cannot be keyed to one letter. The Cabinet is not part of the Parliament: it is the political executive, drawn from members of Parliament and answerable to them, but constitutionally a separate organ. Ministers sit in the House because they are members of it, not because the Cabinet is a limb of it. And a person from outside Parliament can be appointed to the Cabinet. Article 75(5) says a Minister who for six consecutive months is not a member of either House ceases to be a Minister at the end of that period, a rule that only makes sense if such an appointment is permitted.

question: Which one of the following statements about the composition of the Parliament is not correct?
opt_a: Representatives of the states in Rajya Sabha are elected directly by the people.
opt_b: Representatives from Union Territories in Lok Sabha are chosen by direct elections.
opt_d: Lok Sabha has seats reserved for SCs and STs.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Representatives of the states in Rajya Sabha are elected directly by the people. This is the one statement that is untrue. Article 80(4) provides that the representatives of each State in the Council of States shall be elected by the elected members of its Legislative Assembly, by proportional representation through the single transferable vote. The electorate is therefore a few hundred sitting MLAs, not the general public, which is what makes the Rajya Sabha an indirectly elected chamber and the Lok Sabha a directly elected one. The other three statements all hold: twelve members are nominated by the President under Article 80(1)(a), the Lok Sabha reserves seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes under Article 330, and members from the Union territories reach the Lok Sabha by direct election.

question: Which among the following fundamental rights is/are available to non-citizens? 1. Freedom of speech 2. Protection against self-incrimination 3. Freedom of conscience 4. Non-discrimination in matters of employment Select the correct answer using the code given below:
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, 2 and 3 only. The test is the opening words of each article. Article 20(3) says that no person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself, so protection against self-incrimination reaches everyone within India, citizen or not. Article 25(1) entitles all persons equally to freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion. Both therefore run to non-citizens. The other two are worded for citizens alone. Article 19(1) opens with all citizens shall have the right, which covers freedom of speech and expression. Article 16(1) guarantees equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State, and clause (2) bars discrimination against a citizen on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth or residence.

question: Which one of the following statements about the Vice-President of India is not correct?
opt_a: He is not eligible for re-election.
opt_b: He must not be less than 35 years of age.
opt_c: He is elected by members of an electoral college consisting of members of both Houses of Parliament.
opt_d: His term of office is five years.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, He is not eligible for re-election. Nothing in the Constitution bars a Vice-President from a second term, and the office has in fact been held twice by the same person: Mohammad Hamid Ansari served from August 2007 to August 2017. The other three statements come straight from the text. Article 66(3)(b) requires that a person have completed the age of thirty-five years to be eligible.
