Article 66(1) provides that the Vice-President is elected by members of an electoral college consisting of the members of both Houses of Parliament, by proportional representation through the single transferable vote and by secret ballot. Article 67 fixes the term at five years from the date of entering office.

question: A motion of no-confidence is moved against
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, the Council of Ministers. A motion of no confidence is directed at the government as a body, not at any one person in it. Under Rule 198 of the Rules of Procedure of the Lok Sabha it is a motion expressing want of confidence in the Council of Ministers; it needs the leave of the House, with at least fifty members rising in their places to support the request, and it need not set out any grounds. The reason it must target the whole Council is Article 75(3), which makes the Council collectively responsible to the House of the People: if the House withdraws its confidence, every Minister goes, including the Prime Minister.

question: Which one of the following is correct about ‘Pinaka’?
opt_a: It is a multi-barrel rocket system.
opt_b: It is a type of battle tank.
opt_d: It is an indigenously developed drone system.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, It is a multi-barrel rocket system. Pinaka is a truck-mounted multiple launch rocket system developed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation, with design work from the mid-1980s and prototypes by 1992. A battery is built around six launcher vehicles carrying twelve rockets each, with loader and replenishment vehicles and two command post vehicles behind them, and it can put all seventy-two rockets into the air in about forty-four seconds: saturation fire over an area rather than precision against a point. It was used in the Kargil operations of 1999 against Pakistani positions on the heights, and the first regiment was raised in February 2000.

question: Which one of the following is not a member of the Quad group of nations?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, France. The Quadrilateral Security Dialogue has four members and France is not one of them: they are India, the United States, Australia and Japan. The grouping was proposed by the Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe in 2007, lapsed the following year when Australia withdrew, and was revived on the margins of the ASEAN meetings at Manila in 2017. Its first leaders' summit was held virtually on 24 March 2021, six weeks after this paper was set, and the four have met at leader level regularly since. France cooperates with India in the Indian Ocean through separate arrangements (a naval exercise of its own and a trilateral with India and Australia) which is what makes it a plausible-looking wrong answer.

question: The first phase of Exercise Malabar, 2020 was conducted at
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Visakhapatnam. The 24th edition of Malabar was split into two phases in November 2020, and the Indian Navy announced Phase 1 as taking place off Visakhapatnam in the Bay of Bengal from 3 to 6 November 2020. Phase 2 followed in the Arabian Sea from 17 to 20 November. What made the edition significant was the participants: Australia joined India, the United States and Japan, so all four navies exercised together for the first time in thirteen years. Phase 1 brought in the destroyer USS John S McCain, the frigate HMAS Ballarat with an MH-60 helicopter and the Japanese destroyer JS Onami with an SH-60, alongside Indian units; Phase 2 put two carrier battle groups to sea, INS Vikramaditya and USS Nimitz. Because of the pandemic the whole exercise was run as a non-contact, at-sea-only event with no port visits.

question: Hollywood actor Sir Sean Connery, who died recently, was popularly known for the portrayal of the role
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, James Bond. Sean Connery was the first actor to play Ian Fleming's secret agent on screen, in Dr. No in 1962, and returned in From Russia with Love, Goldfinger, Thunderball, You Only Live Twice, Diamonds Are Forever and, outside the main series, Never Say Never Again in 1983. He died at his home at Lyford Cay near Nassau in the Bahamas on 31 October 2020, aged 90: three months before this paper was set, which is why the stem says recently. He won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for The Untouchables in 1987 and was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II at Holyrood Palace on 5 July 2000.

question: The Luhri Hydro-Electric Power Project is being constructed on the river
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Satluj. Luhri Stage-I is a 210 MW hydro-electric project on the Satluj in the Shimla and Kullu districts of Himachal Pradesh, built by SJVN Limited, the joint venture of the Government of India and the Government of Himachal Pradesh. The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs cleared an investment of about 1,810 crore rupees for it in November 2020, three months before this paper was set, which is why the project was in the news; the design output is roughly 758 million units of electricity a year and construction was expected to run to the middle of this decade. SJVN's other stations on the same river are Nathpa Jhakri at 1,500 MW and Rampur at 412 MW.

question: ‘CARAT Bangladesh 2020’ was a joint naval exercise between Bangladesh and
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, USA. CARAT stands for Cooperation Afloat Readiness and Training, and it is a United States Pacific Fleet programme, not an Indian or a regional one. The United States Navy has run it since 1995 as a series of annual bilateral exercises with the navies of South and South-East Asia: Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Sri Lanka and Thailand among them. Bangladesh joined the programme in 2010 and the first CARAT Bangladesh was held in September 2011, and the exercise has been conducted with the United States Navy in the Bay of Bengal every year since.

question: Peninsula Shield Force is a military arm of
opt_b: Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Gulf Cooperation Council. The Peninsula Shield Force was created in 1984 as the joint military arm of the Gulf Cooperation Council, the six-member grouping of Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates founded on 25 May 1981 with its secretariat at Riyadh. The force is stationed near King Khalid Military City at Hafar al Batin in Saudi Arabia, close to the Kuwaiti and Iraqi borders, and by 2011 numbered roughly 40,000 troops drawn from all member states. It has been used three times to note: about 3,000 personnel in the liberation of Kuwait in 1990-91, a 10,000-strong deployment to Kuwait during the Iraq war of 2003, and an intervention in Bahrain in 2011.

question: Which one of the following ships was involved in ‘Mission Sagar – II’?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, INS Airavat. Airavat is a Shardul-class tank landing ship commissioned into the Eastern Naval Command at Visakhapatnam on 19 May 2009, and under Mission Sagar-II in November 2020 she carried food aid to Sudan, South Sudan, Djibouti and Eritrea. The II in the name marks it as a later leg of a series of humanitarian deliveries India made across the Indian Ocean and its approaches through 2020, when the pandemic had disrupted supply lines to smaller and poorer states. A landing ship is the right platform for this work because she can carry bulk cargo and put it ashore where port facilities are limited.

question: In the year 2020 which one of the following tiger reserves of India was declared by UNESCO as a Biosphere Reserve?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Panna Tiger Reserve. The Panna Biosphere Reserve, spread over about 2,999 square kilometres in the Panna and Chhatarpur districts of Madhya Pradesh, was added to UNESCO's World Network of Biosphere Reserves in 2020: India's twelfth entry on that network at the time. The Ken flows for some seventy-two kilometres through the park. Panna also carries one of the better-known conservation stories in the country: its tigers were wiped out by poaching around 2009, animals were brought in from other reserves that year, breeding began in 2010, and the population has since been rebuilt into one of the more successful big-cat restorations anywhere.

question: The Kaleshwaram Lift Irrigation System, which was in the news recently, is constructed in
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Telangana. The Kaleshwaram Lift Irrigation System is built on the Godavari at Kaleshwaram in the Bhupalpally district of Telangana, and was opened on 21 June 2019 by the Governor and the Chief Minister of the state. It is a lift scheme rather than a gravity one (water is pumped up in stages through barrages, pump houses, tunnels and reservoirs rather than being carried down a slope) and at a construction cost of about 80,190 crore rupees, a network of roughly 500 kilometres and a command spread across thirteen districts, it is described as the largest multi-stage lift irrigation project in the world. Its scale is also why it has drawn scrutiny.

question: Cell wall is not present in cells of
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Humans. A cell wall is a rigid layer laid down outside the plasma membrane, and animal cells never build one. A human cell is bounded by its plasma membrane and nothing else, which is why our tissues bend, why a white blood cell can crawl between the cells of a vessel wall, and why a red cell can fold itself through a capillary narrower than its own diameter. The other three organisms in the list all wall themselves in, and each uses a different material: bacteria use peptidoglycan, plants use cellulose, fungi use chitin. That difference in chemistry is exactly what medicine exploits: penicillin blocks the cross-linking of bacterial peptidoglycan, so it wrecks the bacterium and leaves our own cells untouched, because there is no wall in us for it to attack.

question: A child receives a tall beautiful plant as a birthday gift from his father with a quiz. The father asked her how she would verify whether this tall plant was the progeny of both the tall parents or one tall and one short parent plant. She could verify this through
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, self-pollination. Height in the classic pea experiments is set by one gene with a dominant tall allele, so a tall plant can be either pure-breeding (TT) or a hybrid (Tt), and the two look identical. Selfing settles it in one generation. Pollinate the plant with its own pollen: if it is TT, every offspring gets a T from both sides and every offspring is tall. If it is Tt, a quarter of the offspring receive t from both sides and grow short. Short plants in the next generation therefore prove one grandparent was short; a whole crop of tall ones points to two tall parents. The gift plant is the only material the child has, and self-pollination is the one method on the list that needs nothing else and produces a segregating generation.

question: A student was doing an experiment on increasing the cell division among plants. She asked her supervisor to suggest the specific plant hormone for the same. Had you been her supervisor, which plant hormone would you suggest?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Cytokinin. Cytokinins are the class of plant hormones that promote cell division: the name is built on cytokinesis, the division of the cell itself. The first one found, kinetin, was isolated in 1954 from autoclaved herring sperm DNA and named for exactly that power; the first natural one, zeatin, came out of maize endosperm about a decade later and takes its name from Zea, the maize genus. Cytokinins are made chiefly in the roots and move up to the shoot, and they are richest where division is fastest: root tips, developing fruits and seeds. In tissue culture a high cytokinin-to-auxin ratio is what pushes a callus into forming shoots. A supervisor asked for the hormone that raises the rate of cell division has one honest answer on this list.

question: Which cell organelles have their own DNA and Ribosomes?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Mitochondria and Plastids. These two organelles carry a small circular DNA of their own and their own ribosomes, so each can make some of its own proteins independently of the nucleus. That oddity is the strongest evidence for the endosymbiotic account of their origin: they descend from free-living bacteria that were engulfed by an early eukaryotic cell and kept, which also explains their double membrane and the fact that they arise only by division of existing ones rather than being built afresh. Their ribosomes are of the smaller 70S bacterial type, not the 80S type found in the surrounding cytoplasm. One consequence a student meets later is that mitochondrial disorders pass down the maternal line alone, because the sperm's mitochondria are destroyed after fertilisation.

question: Osmosis is the process of movement of water molecules from its
opt_a: higher concentration to its lower concentration through a cell wall.
opt_b: lower concentration to its higher concentration through a fully permeable membrane.
opt_c: higher concentration to its lower concentration through a fully permeable membrane.
opt_d: higher concentration to its lower concentration through a semi-permeable membrane.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, higher concentration to its lower concentration through a semi-permeable membrane. Two conditions have to be met at once. The membrane must be semi-permeable, letting water through while holding back the dissolved solute: a fully permeable membrane lets everything pass and gives ordinary diffusion, not osmosis. And the movement of the water must be described from where water is more concentrated to where water is less concentrated, which is what this option says: 'water molecules from its higher concentration to its lower concentration'. That is the same direction as the familiar statement 'from dilute solution to concentrated solution', because a dilute solution is one where water is abundant and solute scarce. Only option (d) gets both the direction of the water and the nature of the membrane right.

question: Growing of two or more crops simultaneously on the same field in a definite pattern is known as
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, inter cropping. Three words in the stem decide it: 'simultaneously', 'same field' and 'definite pattern'. Growing two crops together on one field at the same time covers both intercropping and mixed cropping; what separates them is the pattern. In intercropping the crops go in as set rows: one row of the second crop after every one, two or three rows of the first, and the ratio is planned in advance. In mixed cropping the seeds of the two crops are simply mixed and broadcast together, with no arrangement at all. Intercropping is done to raise yield from the same piece of land, and the two crops are chosen so that their demands differ (different rooting depths, different nutrient needs, different heights) and they can also be harvested and threshed separately. Soyabean with maize, and groundnut with sunflower, are the standard Indian examples.

question: When we heat lead nitrate [Pb(NO₃)₂] in a boiling tube, we observe the emission of brown fumes. Which one of the following is the brown gas?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, NO₂. Heating lead(II) nitrate breaks it up into three products at once: 2Pb(NO₃)₂ → 2PbO + 4NO₂ + O₂. Of these, the lead(II) oxide stays behind in the tube as a yellow residue and the oxygen is colourless, so the only thing that can be giving the brown fumes is the nitrogen dioxide. NO₂ is the standard brown gas of school chemistry, and this reaction is the standard laboratory way of making it. The demonstration is used to teach thermal decomposition (one compound broken by heat into two or more simpler substances) and it is one of the few school reactions where a coloured gas announces the result across the room.

question: Which one of the following substances do silver articles react with, that makes the silver articles black?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Sulphur. Silver left in the open slowly dulls and blackens, and the black coating is silver sulphide, Ag₂S . It forms because air carries traces of hydrogen sulphide , and silver reacts with that sulphur compound at room temperature. Silver is a noble metal and resists ordinary oxidation, so oxygen is not what blackens it. That is why silver keeps its shine indoors in clean dry air and loses it fast near cooking gas, boiled eggs, rubber bands or industrial fumes. The layer is thin and self-limiting: once formed, it protects the metal beneath, which is why a tarnished spoon can be cleaned back to brightness without losing measurable silver.

question: Which one of the following metals is kept immersed in Kerosene oil to protect it and to prevent accidental fire?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Sodium. Sodium is an alkali metal and among the most reactive of all metals. Left in the open it reacts with the oxygen and moisture of the air, and its reaction with water is violent enough to be dangerous: it produces sodium hydroxide and hydrogen, and the heat released is enough to set the escaping hydrogen alight. That is the accidental fire the question refers to. Kerosene is the standard storage medium because it is a liquid hydrocarbon that does not react with sodium and keeps both air and water vapour off the metal surface, and because sodium is denser than kerosene it stays submerged. Potassium is kept the same way. The paper's own wording, 'to protect it and to prevent accidental fire', names both jobs the kerosene is doing.

question: A solution contains 20 g of solute in 180 g of solvent. If the solvent is water, what is the concentration of the solution in terms of mass by mass percentage?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, 10%. Mass by mass percentage is the mass of solute expressed as a percentage of the mass of the whole solution, and the whole solution is solute plus solvent. Here the solute is 20 g and the solvent 180 g, so the solution weighs 20 + 180 = 200 g. The concentration is (20 ÷ 200) × 100 = 10%. The single step that decides the question is remembering to add the two masses before dividing. Every wrong option in the list is what comes out of dividing by the wrong quantity.

question: Which one of the following elements is a non-metal but is lustrous?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Iodine. Non-metals are normally dull, and iodine is the standard exception every textbook names: solid iodine is a semi-lustrous, greyish-violet solid with a distinctly metallic sheen, even though it is a non-metal: the fourth halogen and the heaviest of the stable ones. Its other properties are firmly non-metallic. It is brittle rather than malleable, it does not conduct electricity, and it is famous for going almost straight from solid to violet vapour on warming, which is the classroom demonstration of sublimation. Iodine matters as the counter-example: physical properties describe a general trend for metals and non-metals, not a law, and this element is the exception the trend is taught with.

question: Which one of the following metals has both malleability and ductility properties?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Au. Gold is the most malleable metal known: a single gram can be beaten into a sheet about a square metre in area, and gold leaf can be made thin enough to be semi-transparent. It is the most ductile as well: gold can be drawn into a wire one atom wide and then stretched further before it snaps. Malleability is the ability to be hammered into sheets and ductility the ability to be drawn into wire, and gold holds the record for both, which is why gold leaf covers domes and manuscripts and why fine gold wire is used for the connections inside microchips. Both properties are properties of a solid metal, and that fact alone removes one of the wrong options here.

question: We are given three copper wires of different lengths and different areas of cross-section. Which one of the following would have highest resistivity?
opt_a: Copper wire of 50 cm length and 1 mm diameter
opt_b: Copper wire of 25 cm length and 0·5 mm diameter
opt_c: Copper wire of 10 cm length and 2·0 mm diameter
opt_d: All the wires would have same resistivity
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, all the wires would have same resistivity. Resistivity is a property of the material, not of the piece of material. It is fixed once the substance and the temperature are fixed, and it does not care how long the wire is or how thick. All three wires in this question are copper, so all three share one value of resistivity. What changes with the dimensions is the resistance, through R = ρL/A: a longer wire has more resistance, a thicker one has less. Doing the arithmetic makes the difference vivid. Taking areas as πd²/4, the quantity L/A works out to about 6.4 × 10⁵ per metre for the first wire, 1.27 × 10⁶ for the second and 3.2 × 10⁴ for the third: resistances in the ratio 20 : 40 : 1. Had the question asked which wire has the highest resistance, the answer would have been the second one; it asks for resistivity, and there the three are equal.

question: Which of the following statements about ‘fission’ is correct? 1. It is related with the creation of new individuals by means of cell division in unicellular organism. 2. It is related with the transformation of heavier nuclei into smaller nuclei. 3. It is related with the creation of a heavier nuclei by means of combining two higher nuclei. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, 1 and 2 only. The word 'fission' means splitting, and it is used in two different sciences with the same core sense. Statement 1 gives the biological use: in single-celled organisms such as Amoeba and Paramecium the parent cell divides into two daughter cells in binary fission, and in the malarial parasite one cell breaks into many in multiple fission: new individuals produced by division of the cell. Statement 2 gives the nuclear use: a heavy nucleus such as uranium-235 splits into lighter nuclei with a release of energy, which is what powers a reactor and the uranium bomb. Statement 3 describes the opposite process. Building a heavier nucleus by combining lighter ones is fusion, the reaction that runs the Sun and the hydrogen bomb, and calling it fission inverts the meaning of the word.

question: Which one of the following is an electric conductor?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Human body. The human body conducts electricity because it is mostly water carrying dissolved salts: sodium, potassium, chloride and other ions in blood, sweat and tissue fluid. Free ions can move, and moving charge is current, so the body offers a path for current rather than blocking it. This is not a laboratory curiosity: it is the reason an electric shock is dangerous, the reason electricians wear rubber gloves and stand on dry wooden platforms, and the reason wet skin is far more hazardous than dry skin, since sweat lowers the body's resistance sharply. The other three options are the standard insulators of the syllabus: plastic, dry wood and, less obviously, pure water.

question: A non-spherical shining spoon can generally be considered as a
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Parabolic mirror. A spoon is a shiny curved reflecting surface: its inner face works as a concave mirror and its outer face as a convex one, which is why your reflection in the bowl of a spoon is upside down on one side and upright on the other. The stem removes the usual approximation by saying the spoon is non-spherical, and among the four options that leaves only one curved-mirror choice. The shape is also physically apt: a spoon bowl is deeper and narrower than a sphere would be, closer to a paraboloid, and a paraboloid is the surface that brings a parallel beam to a single sharp focus without the blurring that a spherical mirror suffers at its edges. The same geometry is used deliberately in torch and headlight reflectors, satellite dishes and reflecting telescopes.

question: Who amongst the following is a pioneer in discovering the heating effect of electric current?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, James P. Joule. James Prescott Joule established in the 1840s that a current passing through a resistance produces heat in a fixed and measurable amount, a result now written as H = I²Rt: the heat produced goes as the square of the current, directly as the resistance, and directly as the time. That relation is Joule's law of heating, and it explains every device that turns electricity into warmth: the electric iron, the room heater, the geyser, the filament lamp and the fuse. Joule also measured the mechanical equivalent of heat, showing that a given amount of work always yields the same quantity of heat, and the SI unit of energy carries his name for that body of work.

question: Which one of the following laws of electromagnetism does not give the direction of magnetic field?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction. Three of the four entries are hand rules , and a hand rule exists to fix a direction in space. The right-hand thumb rule does it most directly: grip the wire with the right hand, thumb along the current, and the curled fingers give the direction of the magnetic field circling it. Fleming's two rules each set field, current and motion at right angles on three fingers, so knowing any two gives the third, including the field. Faraday's law is a quantitative statement: the emf induced in a circuit is proportional to the rate at which the magnetic flux through it changes. It fixes how big the induced emf is, not which way anything points. The direction of the induced current comes from a separate statement, Lenz's law.

question: An antibiotic is not useful against a virus whereas a vaccine is. Which one of the following is the most appropriate reason for this?
opt_a: An antibiotic can break RNA only, whereas virus has DNA.
opt_b: An antibiotic is a carbohydrate in its chemical nature, whereas a vaccine is a protein which works well to kill a virus.
opt_c: Only a vaccine can break the genetic material of a virus.
opt_d: A virus does not use biochemical pathways which can be blocked by an antibiotic. But a vaccine can boost an immune system to fight the virus.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, A virus does not use biochemical pathways which can be blocked by an antibiotic. But a vaccine can boost an immune system to fight the virus. An antibiotic works by jamming a piece of machinery that a bacterium runs and a human cell does not: the building of a peptidoglycan cell wall, protein assembly on the bacterial 70S ribosome, the making of folic acid, the unwinding of bacterial DNA. A virus owns none of that. Outside a cell it is little more than genetic material in a protein coat, and inside a cell it borrows the host's own machinery, so there is no separate viral pathway for the drug to attack without wrecking the patient's cells too. A vaccine takes an entirely different route: it presents the immune system with a harmless form of the antigen, the body makes antibodies and memory cells, and on real exposure the response comes fast enough to prevent disease. The drug attacks the microbe; the vaccine prepares the patient.

question: 'Sleeping sickness' is caused by
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Trypanosoma. African sleeping sickness is caused by the protozoan Trypanosoma brucei, in two human-infecting subspecies: T. b. gambiense, which produces a slow chronic illness in West and Central Africa and accounts for the great majority of cases, and T. b. rhodesiense, which produces an acute illness in East and Southern Africa. The parasite is passed on by the bite of the tsetse fly, Glossina. The disease runs in two stages: first fever, headache, itching and joint pain as the parasite multiplies in the blood and lymph, then, once it crosses into the central nervous system, confusion, unsteadiness and the wrecked sleep pattern that gives the illness its name. The other three names in the list are all protozoa too, which is what makes the question a genuine test rather than a giveaway.

question: Which one among the following is a free living animal?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Planaria. Planarians are free-living flatworms : they occur in fresh water, in the sea and in damp soil, moving over surfaces on their own and feeding on small prey and dead matter rather than living inside another animal. They belong to the phylum Platyhelminthes, class Turbellaria, and are best known for regeneration : cut a planarian and each piece can rebuild the whole animal, from fragments estimated at as little as one part in a few hundred of the original. Every other name in this question is a parasite that cannot complete its life without a host.

question: Which one of the following is the structure of a cardiac muscle cell?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Cylindrical, Branched and Uninucleate. Cardiac muscle is the tissue of the heart wall and it borrows features from both of the other muscle types. Its cells are cylindrical and striated like skeletal muscle fibres, which is why the heart contracts with the same rapid, forceful mechanism. But they branch, so that the cells interlock into a continuous network, and each cell normally carries a single central nucleus rather than the many nuclei of a skeletal fibre. Where two cardiac cells meet end to end they are joined by an intercalated disc, and the gap junctions in that disc pass the electrical signal directly from cell to cell, which is how the whole heart contracts as one unit without a nerve reaching every fibre. Involuntary, striated, branched and uninucleate, that combination belongs to cardiac muscle alone.

question: Which one of the following naturally occurring acids is found in abundance in tomato?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Oxalic acid. School chemistry carries a short table of natural sources of acids, and it is that table the paper is quoting: vinegar gives acetic acid, curd lactic acid, lemon and orange citric acid, tamarind tartaric acid, an ant or nettle sting methanoic acid, and tomato oxalic acid. Each pairing is meant to be learnt as a unit, and this question simply asks for the entry against tomato. The acid is genuinely present in the fruit (measurements of raw tomato give roughly 0.05 per cent oxalic acid by fresh weight) though it is worth being straight about the word 'abundance' in the stem: that figure is small next to spinach at about 0.97 per cent or parsley at about 1.70 per cent, so tomato is not an oxalate-rich food in the dietary sense. What the question is testing is the textbook pairing, and against this option list oxalic acid is the entry the table gives.

question: Which one of the following is used in soda-acid fire extinguishers?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Sodium hydrogen carbonate. A soda-acid extinguisher holds a solution of sodium hydrogen carbonate (baking soda, NaHCO₃) with a sealed bottle of sulphuric acid suspended inside it. Inverting or striking the cylinder breaks the seal, the acid mixes with the solution, and the reaction releases carbon dioxide at once. The gas builds pressure and drives the liquid out through the nozzle in a jet, and the carbon dioxide itself smothers the fire by cutting off oxygen, being heavier than air. Baking soda earns its place because the carbonate group gives up carbon dioxide readily on contact with acid, and because it is cheap, stable and harmless: the same property makes it the raising agent in baking and an ingredient in antacids.

question: Which one of the following sodium compounds is used for softening hard water?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Na2CO3. Hard water is water carrying dissolved calcium and magnesium ions, picked up as rain percolates through limestone and gypsum. Sodium carbonate, sold as washing soda in its decahydrate form Na₂CO₃·10H₂O, softens it by supplying carbonate ions that take those metal ions out of solution as insoluble calcium carbonate and magnesium carbonate, which settle out and leave harmless sodium salts behind. Because the precipitation does not depend on driving off any dissolved gas, it works on permanent hardness: the kind caused by sulphates and chlorides, which simple boiling cannot touch. That is the practical point of the compound: temporary hardness can be dealt with by boiling, and washing soda is what is needed for the rest.

question: Calcium oxide reacts vigorously with water to produce slaked lime whose solution is used for white-washing walls. This slaked lime reacts with component (A) in air to form a thin layer of component (B) to give a shiny finish. What are the components (A) and (B)?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, A – CO2 ; B – CaCO3. Two reactions run in sequence. Quicklime (calcium oxide) reacts vigorously with water to give slaked lime (calcium hydroxide), releasing a great deal of heat: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂. That suspension is what is brushed on the wall. Over the next day or two the coating takes up carbon dioxide from the air and turns into calcium carbonate : Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O. Calcium carbonate is the hard, shiny film that gives a whitewashed wall its finish; it is the same substance as limestone and marble, which is why the surface sets firm rather than staying powdery.

question: How many internal reflections of light take place in the formation of primary rainbow?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, 1. A primary rainbow is made by light that undergoes exactly one internal reflection inside each raindrop. Sunlight enters the drop and is refracted at the surface; the refractive index of water is slightly different for each wavelength, so the colours separate as they bend, that is dispersion. The separated light travels to the far side of the drop, where part of it is reflected once off the inside surface, and it then leaves through the front, refracting a second time. The rays emerge most intensely at about 42 degrees from the direction opposite the Sun, which is why the bow is an arc at a fixed angle and why it has red on the outside. Refraction, dispersion, one internal reflection, refraction, that is the whole primary bow.

question: The direction of acceleration in uniform circular motion is along the
opt_b: tangent to the circle at the point of observation.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, direction perpendicular to velocity. In uniform circular motion the speed never changes but the direction of travel does, continuously, and a change in the direction of velocity is an acceleration just as surely as a change in its size. Because the speed is constant, none of that acceleration can lie along the direction of motion: any component along the velocity would speed the body up or slow it down. What is left is a component at right angles to the velocity, and since the velocity is tangential to the circle, perpendicular to it means along the radius, pointing inwards to the centre. That is the centripetal acceleration, of size v²/r, and the force producing it is whatever physically pulls the body inwards: the string for a whirled stone, gravity for a satellite, friction for a car on a bend.

question: The weight of an object is due to
opt_a: the net force acting on it.
opt_b: the total of all forces acting on it irrespective of their directions.
opt_c: the force that it exerts on the ground.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, the force that it exerts on the ground. Weight is measured by weighing, and what a weighing machine registers is the push the body makes on the surface supporting it. Read that way (the operational definition ) the weight of an object is the force it exerts on its support, which is what this option says. This matches the pull of gravity, mg, whenever the body is at rest on a firm floor, because the floor pushes up with as much force as the body presses down. It comes apart in free fall: an astronaut in orbit is still pulled by gravity but presses on nothing, and the scale reads zero, which is what 'weightless' means. Of the four options, only this one describes an actual force that a body has by virtue of gravity.

question: The size of particles being studied in 'nano-technology' is about
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, 1 – 100 nm. The nanoscale is defined as the range of dimensions between about 1 and 100 nanometres, and nanotechnology is the understanding and control of matter at that scale. A nanometre is a thousand-millionth of a metre, so the window runs from a few atoms across to a particle a thousand times smaller than the width of a human hair. The range is not arbitrary. Below it, matter is described as individual atoms and molecules; above it, a material behaves in bulk. Inside it, a substance can behave quite differently from the same substance in a lump: the melting point falls, the colour can change, the surface area per unit mass becomes enormous and quantum effects begin to show.
